explanation.gentle: The chapter says commitment is more than outward submission.
explanation.direct: Obedience theater can look disciplined while still lacking buy-in.
explanation.competitive: If pressure is your whole explanation, you missed the chapter.

questions.prompt: What is happening when old obligations still control the calendar after a new priority is announced?
choices: Hedging is draining force from the chosen work
The team has already proven durable commitment
The chapter says calendars do not matter

explanation.gentle: Hedging lets the old stack stay alive under the new words.
explanation.direct: The chapter uses this mismatch to explain decorative OKRs.
explanation.competitive: If the leftovers still rule the calendar, the new priority is mostly branded intent.

questions.prompt: A team sounds symbolically united but cannot name what work lost protection for the new priority. Which judgment best fits the chapter?
choices: The team has strong buy-in because nobody objected
The team may have symbolic agreement but not real carried commitment
The team should avoid asking what changed

explanation.gentle: Real commitment normally leaves some visible displacement behind it.
explanation.direct: If nothing lost status, the unity may be symbolic instead of operational.
explanation.competitive: Harmony without sacrifice is usually a warning sign here.

questions.prompt: What deeper point does the chapter make about decorative OKRs?
choices: They are priorities that remain visible in language while lacking governing power in behavior
They are useful backups for when teams get tired
They disappear because the company stopped talking about priorities

explanation.gentle: The problem is not absence of priorities but weakness of control.
explanation.direct: Decorative OKRs stay present on the slide while the older stack still governs action.
explanation.competitive: They look official because they were never meant to win real authority.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 6 naturally lead into an alignment chapter next?
choices: Because commitment removes the need for coordination
Because once one team is truly bound to priorities, the next challenge is how multiple committed teams connect
Because company cases end after commitment

explanation.gentle: The bridge asks how committed teams move together.
explanation.direct: After commitment makes priorities real inside one team, alignment becomes the next issue.
explanation.competitive: Once the load is real, coordination becomes the fight.

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill is testing whether chosen priorities became real obligations that changed what the team carries.
coreSkill.direct: This chapter teaches commitment as behavioral buy-in: priorities must govern action and displace older privileges.
coreSkill.competitive: The skill is forcing an official priority to prove it actually took command.

plan.gentle: If a team says one priority matters most, then check what meetings, staffing, or backlog items lost status because of it.
plan.direct: If the objective sounds important but the old stack still owns the week, then audit the hidden privileges that are blocking commitment.
plan.competitive: If the team claims commitment, make it name what got pushed down.

plan.gentle: If a school board chooses one main initiative, then make the schedule show what older projects stopped leading.
plan.direct: If students agree on the priority but keep every legacy project alive, then remove the false first places from the calendar.
plan.competitive: If the board wants credit for commitment, make it pay by cutting protected leftovers.

plan.gentle: If one personal goal matters most, then reorganize the week so it governs what gets postponed and protected.
plan.direct: If you keep praising a goal while nothing loses status for it, then you need a commitment shift, not a motivation speech.
plan.competitive: If the goal never rewrote the week, stop pretending it leads.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within the next day, choose one official priority and write down what it now controls, what lost privilege, and where hedging still survives.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: In the next 24 hours, run one commitment audit: what governs the calendar now, what old work was demoted, and what decorative language still remains?
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Next day: pick one branded priority and expose whether it took power or just got better wording.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, review one priority for signs of real burden rather than stopping at agreement and visibility.
weeklyPractice.direct: Do a weekly commitment check: what changed, what old obligations lost status, and where is symbolic agreement still doing the work?
weeklyPractice.competitive: Every week, catch one place where the slide says yes and the operating system says no.

front.gentle: What makes this a commitment case?
front.direct: Why does the Nuna story matter after the focus case?
front.competitive: What does this company case add after choosing the priorities?

back.gentle: It shows commitment as staying bound to chosen priorities in real company behavior.
back.direct: It turns commitment into a test of whether the priorities actually govern action.
back.competitive: The case asks whether the winners really took power.

front.gentle: How is awareness different from commitment?
front.direct: Why is meeting agreement weaker than commitment?
front.competitive: Why is nodding at the priority not enough?

back.gentle: Awareness can exist before the team carries any burden for the priority.
back.direct: Commitment begins when the priority governs calendars, tradeoffs, and effort.
back.competitive: Agreement is cheap because it does not have to displace anything.

front.gentle: What makes buy-in visible in this chapter?
front.direct: How do you know a team is carrying the chosen priority?
front.competitive: What proof separates real buy-in from branding?

back.gentle: Real buy-in changes what gets postponed or stops being protected.
back.direct: You know it is real when older obligations lose privilege.
back.competitive: Real buy-in leaves visible losses somewhere else in the system.

front.gentle: What is hedging in the chapter logic?
front.competitive: How does the old regime survive under the new words?

back.gentle: Hedging means the old obligations keep their place while the new priority stays mostly symbolic.
back.direct: Decorative OKRs appear when visible priorities never gain real authority.
back.competitive: The team says the new words and obeys the old stack.

front.gentle: Why does the chapter separate commitment from coercion?
front.direct: Why is pressure theater not enough for commitment?
front.competitive: Why can fear fake the surface and still fail the chapter?

back.gentle: Because people need to carry the choice, not merely submit to its language.
back.direct: Forced compliance can mimic order without creating real buy-in.
back.competitive: Pressure can stage commitment while leaving the operating system unchanged underneath.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: The Nuna case shows that commitment becomes real when chosen priorities govern behavior strongly enough to displace old obligations and symbolic agreement.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: A team is committed when the priority takes command of calendars, tradeoffs, and effort instead of remaining decorative language.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: If the old stack still rules the week, the commitment is still theater.
